Photograph: Scott G Winterton/The Deseret News/AP Utah Utah wildfire blocks rescuers from reaching firefighting helicopter crash site Fate of two passengers onboard helicopter that went down Friday morning remains unknown after more than 24 hours Uwa Ede-Osifo Sat 8 Aug 2026 19.43 EDT Last modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 19.44 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The fate of two passengers onboard a firefighting helicopter that crashed Friday morning in Utah remains unknown after more than 24 hours, as one of the country’s largest wildfires continues to grow, preventing authorities from safely reaching the accident site. The Sikorsky S-64 helicopter, contracted by the US Forest Service, was responding on Friday to the Widemouth 2 fire, a blaze sparked in late July by lightning, when it crashed in a remote area of central Utah . Widemouth 2 has swept through more than 114,600 acres (46,400 hectares) and is 24% contained, as of Saturday. That figure marked a jump from early on Friday, where the fire’s scope was reported as reaching more than 105,000 acres, according to state data. The chopper’s crash ignited a new blaze, state authorities said at a news conference on Friday evening. The accident site is within the fire’s perimeter. “Ground resources attempted to respond immediately, but access to the scene was compromised by the emergent fire,” the US Forest Service wrote in a Saturday statement. “Without a safety zone, the Incident Management Team determined not to place lives at risk until the area is deemed safe.” Federal officials have advised the public to refrain from speculating on the nature of the crash, as search-and-rescue teams wait for fire conditions to subside to safer levels. In a Saturday daily report, however, the US National Interagency Fire Center, a coalition of state and federal agencies, said the helicopter’s “pilot and one crewmember were fatally injured”. At a Saturday morning briefing, a moment of silence was observed to honor the passengers. The US Forest Service has declined to confirm their status. “There have already been many false reports and rumors, and the victims deserve the highest level of respect and avoidance of speculation,” the agency wrote. Investigators with the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) were en route to Richfield, a city roughly 160 miles (250km) south of Salt Lake City, as of Friday. When they are able to reach the crash site, they will document the scene, before retrieving the aircraft. The western US states have faced a deadly wildfire season. In June, three firefighters died, as they battled a blaze along the Colorado-Utah border. A fourth firefighter later died from burn injuries sustained during the emergency response. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw99.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, Serhii K was extradited to Germany from Italy late last year By Paul Kirby ,Â Europe digital editor Â and Â Jessica Parker ,Â Berlin correspondent Published 3 hours ago Four years after one of the most dramatic acts of sabotage in modern European history, a Ukrainian man goes on trial in Hamburg on Wednesday accused of blowing up Russia's Nord Stream gas pipelines to Germany. Serhii K, as he is identified by German prosecutors, is accused of plotting with other Ukrainian military personnel to destroy the pipelines and stop Russia financing its war with gas revenue. The case is highly sensitive in Germany, seen as one of Ukraine's closest allies since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, seven months before the attacks took place. Serhii K, extradited to Germany last year, will become the first suspect to go on trial for the blasts. He denies the charges, as does a second suspect who is fighting extradition from Croatia. In the months after explosives destroyed three of the four gas pipelines in the Baltic Sea off the island of Bornholm on 26 September 2022, Western suspicion looked towards Moscow without directly apportioning blame. Russia had already shut off the flow of gas to Germany in Nord Stream 1 weeks before the attack, and Nord Stream 2 had never been turned on. Berlin had frozen the multi-billion dollar project shortly before the invasion and there were reports of suspicious Russian naval movements before the blasts. As investigators from Sweden, Denmark and Germany tried to find out who carried out the attack, Russia's Vladimir Putin accused the US and its UK allies, blaming "the Anglo-Saxons" - which they denied. Eventually, after Denmark and Sweden shut down their inquiries, German prosecutors focused on a group of deep-sea divers who had rented a yacht called the Andromeda in the northern German port of Rostock. They said later that "traces of subsea explosives were found in the samples taken from the boat". Image source, Swedish Coast Guard Image caption, Three of the four Nord Stream pipelines were ruptured by explosions in September 2022 Despite the strain on relations with Kyiv, German prosecutors pressed ahead with the case, and in January 2025 the German federal court of justice ruled that it fell within German territorial jurisdiction , external and prosecutors had a responsibility to act as it involved "undermining [Germany's] internal security". Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky has always maintained that Ukraine had "nothing to do with [the Nord Stream blasts]", although in their indictment German prosecutors allege the saboteurs conceived the plot "acting by order of Ukrainian state agencies". They say the case falls under Germany's code of crimes against international law as a war crime" as an attack by military means against civilian objects". Nord Stream trial: How German police followed the evidence - to Ukraine Published 3 days ago The case has highlighted differences of opinion on the trial in Kyiv and Berlin. Oleksandr Merezhko, who chairs the Foreign Affairs Committee in the Ukrainian parliament, points out that the blasts took place during a time of war with Russia and "Nord Stream 2 was nothing but a tool used by Russia in order to get prepared for the war". He told the BBC they had no confirmation of the German account: "It's one of the versions." However, Stefan Meister, of the German Council on Foreign Relations, says successive chancellors in Berlin have done their best to remove the politics from the case. "They tried to make not a big story out of it, not to give it too much attention, to give it to the institutions, to the judiciary that they will deal with it. This is not a political case. So they tried to depoliticise it," he explained. In August 2025, Serhii K was arrested after checking into a hotel near the Italian Adriatic resort of Rimini, by police acting under a European arrest warrant issued by federal prosecutors in Germany. After several weeks of court battles fighting extradition, Serhii K - identified in court documents as Serhii Kuznetsov - was transferred to Germany late last year. German prosecutors allege that in 2022 he was a serving officer in the Ukrainian army , external , and he had led a group of professional divers, a boat captain and an explosives expert. While his legal fight was going on in Italy, another Ukrainian man called Volodymyr Zhuravlov successfully challenged Germany's extradition bid in a Polish court. In a ruling very different from Italy's Supreme Court, the Polish judge ordered Zhuravlov's release in October 2025, stating that the attack on the pipelines was not unlawful, and if Ukraine had organised an armed mission it was "justified, rational and just". Although he was released by the court in Warsaw, he was arrested last August in Croatia on suspicion of being a suspect who "participated in the dives necessary" for the sabotage. Last month, Croatia approved his extradition, although it is not clear when that will happen, and if his case could become part of the Hamburg trial. Despite the difficult nature of the case for Kyiv and Berlin, Ukrainian MP Oleksandr Merezhko does not believe it will spoil relations as "it's in the best national interests of Germany to continue to support us".
